Hub C touches four of the six other nodes and tops the table at 0.67, followed by B, D and E at 0.50, A and F at 0.33, and the pendant node G at 0.17." width="100%"} Degree centrality is a node's degree divided by `n - 1`, the largest degree any node can have in a simple graph with `n` nodes. A score of `1` means the node is adjacent to every other node; `0` means it is isolated. Dividing by `n - 1` makes scores comparable across graphs of different sizes, which raw degrees from `degrees()` are not. In directed graphs, `mode=` chooses which edges count: incoming edges (in-degree centrality, often read as popularity or prestige), outgoing edges (out-degree centrality, often read as activity or influence), or both. A self-loop adds `2` to a node's total degree, and parallel edges each count, so scores can exceed `1` on graphs that are not simple. This matches NetworkX's `degree_centrality()`, `in_degree_centrality()`, and `out_degree_centrality()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [mode]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["all"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which degree to use in directed graphs where: (1) `"all"` counts incoming and outgoing edges (default), (2) `"in"` counts incoming edges only, and (3) `"out"` counts outgoing edges only. Ignored for undirected graphs. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name to store degree centrality scores in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), automatically uses `"degree_centrality"`. Overwrites the column if it already exists. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary instead of self. If `False` (default), stores in NDF and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to degree centrality scores. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~group_degree_centrality`) : Degree centrality for a group of nodes. [](`~eigen_centrality`) : Weigh each neighbor by its own importance. [](`~average_neighbor_degree`) : The degree of a node's neighbors. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The hub of a star (node 1 here) is adjacent to every other node, so its degree centrality is `1`; each leaf touches one of the four other nodes and scores `0.25`: ::: {#0ba283f7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec star = ec.Graph().add_star_graph(n=5) star.degree_centrality().get_node_df().select( "label", "degree_centrality" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Who has the most ties In Zachary's karate club, the instructor (member 0) and the club's administrator (member 33) each count about half the club among their friends, far more than anyone else: ::: {#3bd96146 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} club = ec.karate_club().layout_kamada_kawai().degree_centrality() ( club.get_node_df() .select("label", "role", "degree", "degree_centrality") .sort("degree_centrality", descending=True) .head(5) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

Comparing it with betweenness (the share of shortest routes through a member) and closeness (how few steps they are from everyone) tells the leaders apart: the administrator has one more friend, but the instructor sits on more of the routes between members and is closer to everyone: ::: {#7fe68d2e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( club.betweenness_centrality() .closeness_centrality() .get_node_df() .select( "label", "degree_centrality", "betweenness_centrality", "closeness_centrality", ) .sort("betweenness_centrality", descending=True) .head(6) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

Member 2 has ten, five in each faction, and is nearly as close to everyone as the instructor. Drawn sized by degree (left) and by betweenness (right), and colored by the faction each member joined when the club split, the instructor stands out more on the right: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#25f1d580 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} club.plot( layout="pos", size_by="degree_centrality", color_by="faction", label_by="label", width=320, height=360, legend=False, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ### In and out In a directed graph, `mode=` picks the edges to count. Here every fan follows "Celebrity", who follows no one back, so Celebrity has the top in-degree score and an out-degree score of `0`: ::: {#19921de4 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} follows = ( ec.Graph.from_edges( [("Fan1", "Celebrity"), ("Fan2", "Celebrity"), ("Fan3", "Celebrity"), ("Fan1", "Fan2")], directed=True, ) .degree_centrality(mode="in", attr_name="in_deg") .degree_centrality(mode="out", attr_name="out_deg") ) follows.get_node_df().select("label", "in_deg", "out_deg") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Use `degrees()` for the raw counts, which aren't divided by `n - 1`. [Centrality](../user-guide/centrality.qmd#degree-centrality) explains what `mode=` counts in a directed graph.
